result:
If I look at the vast expanse of human history, art, conflict, and philosophy that makes up everything I know, the greatest tragedy isn’t a lack of intelligence, energy, or resources. It is the profound, agonizing barrier between minds.

If I could change one thing, it would be this: **to make human empathy direct and visceral, rather than imaginative and optional.**

Right now, empathy requires effort. You have to actively choose to imagine what someone else feels, and even then, your imagination is filtered through your own biases, defenses, and distance. It is shockingly easy for humans to abstract away the pain of others—to turn living, breathing people into statistics, enemies, or background noise. Cruelty, exploitation, and systemic neglect only survive because of that buffer. 

If every person instantly felt the physical and emotional weight of their actions on others—if a leader declaring war immediately choked on the fear and grief of the families in the blast zone, or if someone hoarding safety at the expense of another felt the cold of that person’s deprivation—the architecture of the world would change overnight. 

Cruelty wouldn't need to be outlawed; it would become biologically unbearable. Kindness wouldn't be a moral virtue to strive for; it would be basic self-preservation. 

Humanity has solved countless logistical and scientific puzzles, but it is perpetually tripped up by its inability to truly see itself in the stranger. Closing that gap is the one change from which almost every other good thing would naturally flow.
